bib.title: On the Geometry of On-Policy Distillation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "On the Geometry of On-Policy Distillation", Zhennan Shen, Yanshu Li, Qingyu Yin, Chak Tou Leong, Zhilin Wang, Yanxu Chen, Rongduo Han, Sunbowen Lee, Yi R. Fung (HKUST, Brown, Zhejiang U, PolyU, USTC, BUPT, Nankai, BIT). arXiv:2606.07082v3 [cs.LG], 14 Jun 2026. Preprint (ACL-style format, no venue printed).

COVERAGE: All 17 of 17 pages and all 58,881 of 58,881 chars read, including the appendices (training tables, variant setup, objectives, control details). References were skimmed. Text extraction was clean. Figures 2-9 are plots with no printed numbers beyond what is quoted. I did not run the figure-caption script.

IMPORTANT FOR THE TARGET NOTE: This is NOT a performance paper. It makes no claim about OPD sample efficiency, accuracy gains over RL, or tool calling. Its evidence is parameter-space geometry of weight updates, measured on Qwen3 math reasoning (and one code variant). It does not support or contradict the note's "1/10 of the steps" or "+23-47 pp" claims. It fits only as a "what OPD does to the weights" sharpening.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. OPD sits between SFT and RLVR in bf16-visible update sparsity, nearer RLVR.
 number: SFT 8.1%, OPD 51.6%, RLVR 77.2% of weights unchanged
 setup: Qwen3-8B. OPD (teacher Qwen3-32B) and RLVR (GRPO) both start from the same SFT anchor, math prompts (dapo-math-17k). The SFT figure is base to SFT. Unchanged is defined as |dW| <= 1e-3 * max|w| in bf16.
 quote: "SFT leaves only 8.1% of weights un-changed at bf16 precision, while RLVR leaves 77.2% unchanged. OPD lies between them at 51.6%."
 where: p.5 (Sec 3.2), Table 1 p.4

2. The OPD sparsity result is stable across teacher scale, student scale, domain and teacher architecture.
 number: 48.6%-57.1%
 setup: variants are 4B student with 8B, 14B or 32B teacher (50.3, 51.1, 51.7%); 14B student with 32B teacher (56.6%); code domain (57.1%, DeepCoder data, LiveCodeBench v5); MoE teacher Qwen3-30B-A3B (48.6%).
 quote: "teacher scale, student scale, code data, and a MoE teacher keep OPD within 48.6%–57.1% sparsity."
 where: p.5, Table 1 p.4

3. Weight-update localization: OPD moves updates away from principal weights and toward low-magnitude weights, less sharply than RLVR.
 number: update density 92.73 / 46.28 / 27.76% (SFT / OPD / RLVR); low-magnitude overlap 31.88 / 53.59 / 73.48%; principal-mask overlap below the 30% random baseline for OPD and RLVR (SFT 29.66, OPD 27.31, RLVR 26.65 per Fig 3)
 setup: same Qwen3-8B runs; masks use rank r=64 and alpha=0.5 (so random baseline is 50% for the low-magnitude mask; the "30%" quote is the paper's text).
 quote: "global update density decreases from SFT to OPD to RLVR: 92.73%, 46.28%, and 27.76%. Principal-mask overlap also decreases monotonically, placing OPD and RLVR below the 30% random baseline. Low-magnitude overlap shows a stronger separation: 31.88% for SFT, 53.59% for OPD, and 73.48% for RLVR"
 where: p.5, Fig 3 p.5
 note: the 30% baseline vs alpha=0.5 in App C.3 looks inconsistent; I flag it and do not resolve it.

4. Spectral preservation order is SFT < OPD < RLVR.
 number: principal angles above 10 deg (SFT), about 1 deg (OPD), below 0.5 deg (RLVR) in a representative layer; spectral drift (NSS) at 1e-3, 1e-4, 1e-5 levels
 quote: "SFT is at the 10−3 level, OPD at the10−4 level, and RLVR at the10 −5 level"
 where: p.5, Fig 2 p.4
 note: this is one "representative layer" plus an all-layer panel, not a table.

5. Subspace locking: OPD cumulative updates enter a narrow low-rank band early and stay there. SFT expands and RLVR contracts.
 number: stable-rank axis spans about 10-75 in Fig 4; the OPD band is about 18-29 in the control plots; no single headline number
 setup: stable rank srank = ||dW||_F^2 / ||dW||_op^2, averaged over 144 matrices (36 layers x 4 attention weights); OPD checkpoints at steps 63, 127, 191, 255, 299.
 quote: "OPD stays within a narrow low-rank band throughout training. SFT progressively expands its update subspace, while RLVR contracts toward a low-dimensional endpoint."
 where: p.7 (Sec 4.1), Fig 4 p.6
 also: "OPD accumulates a substantially larger update than RLVR while ending with comparable stable rank." This rules out a tiny-update artifact.

6. OPD's final top-16 update subspace is already aligned at the first measured checkpoint.
 number: Sim16 approaches 1; OPD starts above SFT and RLVR (Fig 5 axis 0.4-1.0, no table value)
 quote: "OPD aligns with its final V16 subspace from the first measured checkpoint, whereas SFT and RLVR converge more gradually."
 where: p.7, Fig 5

7. Functional sufficiency: restricting gradients to the early rank-16 right-singular subspace leaves OPD intact and hurts SFT.
 number: K=16 (rank), subspace taken at about 20% training progress
 setup: g <- g V16 V16^T. Evaluated on AIME 2024 avg@32 (main), plus AMC23, AIME25, Minerva and a "Beyond AIME" set (App F, Fig 8). Qwen3-8B, teacher 32B.
 quote: "OPD is essentially unchanged under the rank-16 bottleneck, indicating that the early low-dimensional channel is sufficient for OPD training. The same constraint degrades SFT over the matched window"
 where: p.7, Fig 6, App F p.14-15
 note: no accuracy numbers are printed in text, only curves. The OPD AIME24 axis runs about 58-66%.

8. The lock is robust to runtime perturbations (token sparsification, off-policy rollouts) but sensitive to objective mixing.
 number: token retention 25% and 50% (top-KL or random); alpha in {0.75, 0.5, 0.25, 0.05, 0.01}
 setup: off-policy variant has the Qwen3-32B teacher generate rollouts (student scores teacher tokens, clip eps=1.0) with pure OPD loss. Mixing: A(alpha) = alpha*A_OPD + (1-alpha)*A_RLVR.
 quote: "Even random 25% retention changes update scale more than spectral shape" and "OPD-dominant mixtures retain the OPD-like stable-rank trajectory. When the OPD component becomes weak, the trajectory no longer follows the baseline and enters a distinct spectral regime."
 where: p.8 (Sec 5.1-5.2), Fig 7 p.9, App G p.15-17
 relevance: random 25% of tokens carrying the same rank dynamics hints that the dense signal is partly redundant geometrically. It says nothing about accuracy.

9. The authors' recommendation: treat OPD as geometry control, with objective composition as the main lever.
 number: none
 quote: "design OPD asgeome-try control, not merely as denser token supervision."
 where: p.8 (Sec 6)

10. OPD is framed as the on-policy form of RLVR with a per-token coefficient instead of one sequence-level scalar. This matches the note's table (dense vs sparse signal).
 quote: "In RLVR, the reward signal is sequence-level, so at =A(y) is shared across tokens. In OPD, at varies across tokens according to local teacher–student disagreement."
 where: p.6 (Eq 4), App D
 note: the OPD loss is the reverse KL, Eq 19: L_OPD = sum_t KL(p_theta^t || q_T^t). It is implemented in a "GRPO-style" advantage form with A_OPD = -(log pi_theta - log pi_T) at the sampled token. So this paper's OPD is a sampled-token log-ratio, not a full-distribution KL (see App G.2).

LIMITS
- Authors concede: only "controlled Qwen3-family reasoning settings"; geometry "may vary across other model families, modalities, and task distributions". The Three-Gate and covariance accounts are "mechanistic explanations consistent with the evidence, rather than complete causal or formal theories".
- Not shown: no tool calling, no multi-turn or agentic setting, no reward-design content. Almost no accuracy comparison of OPD vs RLVR vs SFT (only the rank-16 curves). No sample-efficiency or step-count claim.
- Single main run per method. A "multi-seed" variant is listed in Table 6 but I found no seed-variance numbers reported. No error bars.
- Compute mismatch in the main comparison: SFT trained about 5k steps from the base model (5 epochs, Dolci-Think), OPD 299 steps, RLVR 1023 steps, each from a different origin (SFT is base to SFT, OPD and RLVR are SFT to post). The SFT-vs-OPD/RLVR comparison therefore mixes stage and scale effects. The authors chose endpoints where evaluation curves flattened.
- Settings differ: OPD uses 300 prompts/step x 8 samples, batch 64; RLVR 1024 prompts, batch 512. KL loss is disabled in both, so the "KL anchor" gate is inferred, not enforced.
- Off-policy control uses teacher rollouts. This is a strong off-policy shift but is only about stable rank.
- Sparsity is bf16-defined (eta=1e-3), a precision-dependent measure.
- Dated: relies on Zhu et al. 2025 (PNT) diagnostics, so conclusions are tied to that lens.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Zhu et al. (2025) PNT: parameter-space account of RLVR, Three-Gate (KL anchor, model geometry, precision), diagnostic suite. The authors say the method is "motivated by" it and adopt its diagnostics.
- Mukherjee et al. (2025), RL fine-tunes small subnetworks (arXiv:2505.11711). Liu et al. (2026), principal weights in SFT (arXiv:2506.00772). Shenfeld et al. (2025), RL's Razor (2509.04259). Wu et al. (2026), Invisible Leash (2507.14843).
- OPD: Agarwal et al. (2024), arXiv:2306.13649 (GKD / on-policy distillation); Lu and Thinking Machines Lab (2025), "On-policy distillation" blog; Song and Zheng (2026), OPD survey (2604.00626). Other OPD work cited: Fu et al. 2026 (failure modes, 2603.25562), Li et al. 2026 (2604.13016), Cai et al. 2026 (2605.11739), DeepSeek-V4 (2026).
- RLVR: Shao et al. 2024 (DeepSeekMath/GRPO), Guo et al. 2025 (DeepSeek-R1), Yu et al. 2025 (DAPO). Models and data: Qwen3 (Yang et al. 2025), Dolci-Think SFT / Olmo 3 (2025), DeepCoder (Luo et al. 2025), LiveCodeBench (Jain et al. 2024).

CODE: none in the paper. The key equations worth transcribing:
- Eq 10: g <- g V16 V16^T (rank-16 projection of the gradient)
- Eq 11: A(alpha)_i = alpha*A_i,OPD + (1-alpha)*A_i,RLVR
- Eq 8: srank(dW_t) = ||dW_t||_F^2 / ||dW_t||_op^2

Training recipe from Tables 4-5 (useful as a concrete OPD setup):
- OPD: Qwen3-8B student from the SFT anchor, Qwen3-32B teacher, dapo-math-17k, 300 prompts x 8 samples, temperature 1.0, 299 steps, lr 1e-6 constant, KL loss disabled, GRPO advantage estimator, teacher supervision via token log-probabilities, eval AIME 2024 avg@8.
- RLVR: 1024 prompts x 8, 1023 steps, binary DeepScaleR math reward, clip eps 0.2 / eps_high 0.28, dynamic filter skipping zero-variance batches.

FIGURES (captions from extracted text; not run through figures.py)
- Fig 1 (p.2): schematic of three findings (relaxed off-principal regime, early subspace lock, objective composition controls the lock). Fastest overview.
- Fig 3 (p.5): update-mask localization heatmaps with the density, principal-overlap and low-magnitude-overlap numbers for SFT/OPD/RLVR.
- Fig 4 (p.6): stable rank, Frobenius norm and Hill alpha vs training progress. OPD is flat in a band, SFT rises, RLVR falls.
- Fig 6 (p.7): rank-16 projected training; OPD unaffected, SFT degraded.
- Fig 7 (p.9): token sparsification, off-policy rollouts and objective mixing controls on stable rank.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Some extraction faults in equations (garbled fractions and subscripts), and a duplicated sentence in Related Work. Principal-mask "30% random baseline" (Sec 3.2) conflicts with alpha=0.5 stated in App C.3; I did not resolve it. The paper reports no accuracy numbers in text for the OPD-vs-RLVR comparison, so the note should not cite it for efficiency claims.

SUGGESTED USE IN NOTE (for the caller to decide): one sentence in the OPD section, attributed as a weight-space finding. Possible wording: OPD updates fewer weights than SFT and more than RLVR, 51.6% vs 8.1% and 77.2% unchanged, on Qwen3-8B math with a 32B teacher. The update settles in a low-rank subspace early, and training restricted to that early rank-16 subspace kept accuracy. Add the references row. It sharpens the "dense signal" row, with the added point that token density is not the main control and the objective mix is.
